title: What I've done
goal: Student uses present perfect (have/has + past participle) to talk about life experiences with ever/never; knows the most common past participles.
connects_to: M03 (PP vs past simple) — after PP introduction, learn when to use each.
module_chunks: I've been to... / I've never been to...
I've seen / I've eaten / I've tried / I've visited
past participles: been, seen, done, gone, had, made, eaten, drunk, written, spoken
in my life / so far / before

units.title: Have you ever?
units.real_life_context: You ask and answer about life experiences (travel, food, events).

grammar.explanation: Present perfect with I/you/we/they uses "have" + past participle. "I have visited" or "I've / I have visited".
She/he/it uses "has" + past participle. "She has tried" or "She's / She is tried".
Present perfect question with you: "Have you ever been?".
"I've / I have never seen" — "never" is the standard negative in PP for life experiences.
"I have never tried" — present perfect with I.
"Has she ever traveled?" — she uses "has" in PP question.
"We have never been" — common life experience structure.
After "have/has", use PAST PARTICIPLE: "visited" (not "visit").
She → "has", not "have". 3rd person uses "has" in PP.

grammar.passage: I have visited five countries: Italy, France, Japan, Brazil, and Argentina. I've never been to Australia. My sister has been to Australia twice.
grammar.question: How many countries has the speaker visited?
grammar.explanation: The text says "I have visited five countries".

listening_speaking.text: Have you ever been to Brazil?
I have never seen that movie.
We have never been to Japan.

units.title: I've been to many places
units.real_life_context: You describe travel and life experiences using common irregular past participles.

grammar.explanation: "Been" = visited and returned. "Gone" = went and still there. For experiences (where you've visited), use "been".
"Read" past participle = "read" (same spelling, /red/ pronunciation).
"Eat" → "ate" → "eaten" (past participle).
"Speak" → "spoke" → "spoken".
"See" → "saw" → "seen" (past participle).
"Write" → "wrote" → "written".

grammar.sentence: We have _____ a lot of work.
grammar.explanation: "Do" → "did" → "done".
For experiences = "been". "Gone" = still there. "Went" is past simple (without have).
After has/have, past participle: "eaten", not "ate".

grammar.passage: I have been to ten countries. I've eaten unusual food and met interesting people. My friend has written a book about her travels.
grammar.question: What has the friend done?
grammar.explanation: The text says "My friend has written a book".

units.title: Just, already, yet
units.grammar_focus: just / already / yet with present perfect
units.real_life_context: You talk about recently completed actions and pending tasks.

grammar.explanation: "Just" = a moment ago, recently. Goes between have and past participle.
"Already" = sooner than expected. Between has and past participle.
"Yet" goes at end of QUESTION or NEGATIVE: "Have you finished yet?".
"Yet" at end of negative sentence: "I haven't / have not seen it yet" = ainda não.
"Just" — recent action. "She has just left".

grammar.sentence: I've _____ done my homework — finished an hour ago.
grammar.explanation: "Already" = before now (sooner). "I've / I have already done".
"Have they arrived yet?" — checking if it has happened.

grammar.hint: yet goes at end, not middle
grammar.answer: I haven't seen that movie yet.
grammar.explanation: "Yet" goes at END of negative/question, not between have/has and verb. Used with negative.
After "just", use past participle: "left" (not "leave").

grammar.passage: I've just finished my report. I've already eaten lunch. I haven't called my mom yet — I'll do it soon.
grammar.question: What hasn't the speaker done yet?
grammar.explanation: The text says "I haven't / have not called my mom yet".

listening_speaking.text: She has just left the office.

units.title: Have you been there?
units.grammar_focus: Present perfect questions and short answers
units.real_life_context: You quiz friends about life experiences.

grammar.explanation: PP question with you: "Have you ever been?".
She → "Has". PP question 3rd person.
Plural → "Have".
Short answer: "Yes, I have".
"Has he ever visited?" — 3rd person.
"No, she hasn't / has not" — short negative answer.
"Have you eaten?" — you uses "have".

grammar.sentence: Did you ever been to Japan?
grammar.answer: Have you ever been to Japan?
grammar.explanation: PP questions use "have/has" inverted, NOT "did". "Did" is for past simple.

grammar.sentence: Have you ever go to Italy?
grammar.answer: Have you ever been to Italy?
grammar.explanation: After "Have", use past participle. For experiences = "been" (not "go" or "gone").

grammar.passage: Q: Have you ever traveled solo? A: Yes, I have. Q: Has your sister tried sushi? A: No, she hasn't. She doesn't like fish.
grammar.question: Has the sister tried sushi?
grammar.explanation: The text says "No, she hasn't / has not".

listening_speaking.text: Have you ever been to Italy?
Yes, I have. No, I haven't.

units.title: Life so far
units.real_life_context: You tell a "life so far" summary integrating all PP forms.

grammar.explanation: PP with I uses "have".
Past participle of read = read (same spelling, /red/).
"Never" with PP for life negative.
PP question with you.
"I have just finished" — recent.
"Already" — between has and past participle.
"Yet" at end of negative.
She → "has".
For life experiences, "been" (not "went"). "Went" needs past simple structure.

grammar.passage: I've traveled to five countries. I've never been to Asia. I've just learned that my friend has won a prize.
